title: Theories of International Trade
outcomes: Explain what international trade is, how it differs from internal trade, and weigh the arguments for and against freer trade.
Describe the mercantilist view and Adam Smith's absolute advantage theory with its assumptions.
Apply Ricardo's comparative advantage (and Haberler's opportunity-cost version) to numerical data, including the terms-of-trade range and gains in labour hours.
Explain the Heckscher-Ohlin theory, factor-price equalisation and the new trade theory (economies of scale, network effects, intra-industry trade).

meta.exam_tip: Expect 2–4 MCQs: one or two numericals on absolute/comparative advantage (compute opportunity costs both ways) and theory-matching questions (who said what). Watch the "NOT" in the stem.

concepts.title: International trade, its gains and the case against it
body: International trade means buying and selling goods, services and resources across national borders, between residents of different countries. Compared with internal (domestic) trade it is more complex: several currencies, different legal systems, customs procedures, longer distances, language and cultural differences, and limited mobility of labour and capital between countries.

Why countries trade: a bigger market allows specialisation and division of labour; resources move to their most productive use; domestic monopolies face competition; inputs can be sourced cheaply from anywhere; consumers get more variety at lower prices; trade earns the foreign exchange needed to pay for imports; it pushes automation, research and innovation; it widens the market for services such as banking, insurance and logistics; it helps emerging economies climb the global value chain, diversify exports, share know-how and build friendly relations with other nations.

The case against free trade: gains may be unequal between rich and poor nations; weaker countries may be exploited by powerful global corporations; natural resources may be used up fast and the environment harmed; booms and slumps spread quickly from one country to another; heavy dependence on foreign supplies can threaten economic and even political independence, especially during wars; too much export focus can pull investment away from a country's real needs; and trade partners may suddenly change policy — bans, high tariffs or embargoes.
concepts.analogy: Trade is like a neighbourhood where the baker bakes and the tailor stitches: everyone eats and dresses better than if each did both badly. But if one shop owns the whole street, the others may lose out.
concepts.work: Export-import businesses, their auditors and lenders keep watching for currency risk, sudden policy changes (a duty hike or an import ban) and dependence on one foreign supplier. Spotting these risks early is part of business advisory and going-concern work.

concepts.title: Mercantilism — trade as a way to pile up gold
body: Mercantilism was the dominant economic idea in Europe from roughly the 16th to the 18th century. It held that a nation's wealth and power depended on its stock of gold and silver (precious metals).

So the state should push exports up and keep imports down, aiming for a permanent trade surplus (a favourable balance of trade). Governments controlled industry and trade and put very high tariffs on foreign goods.

Weakness: trade was seen as a zero-sum game — one nation's gain was another's loss. Later economists showed that both trading partners can gain. Traces of mercantilist thinking still appear whenever a country treats a trade surplus as a goal in itself.
concepts.analogy: A shopkeeper who loves selling but refuses to buy anything, counting coins every night — rich in coins, poor in comforts.
concepts.work: When a government announces export push schemes together with import curbs, analysts call it "neo-mercantilist". Understanding the motive helps a CA forecast which sectors will get protection and which will face higher input costs.

concepts.title: Absolute advantage — Adam Smith
body: Adam Smith argued that trade rests on absolute cost differences. A country has an absolute advantage in a good if it can make it with less labour (fewer resources) than another country.
If Country A is absolutely better at one good and Country B at another, each should specialise in its own good and trade; total world output rises and both gain.

Assumptions: two countries and two goods; no transport cost; cost measured by the labour needed (labour theory of value); labour moves freely within a country but not between countries; trade happens only when each country has an absolutely lower cost in one good.
Limitation: if one country is absolutely better at both goods, the theory predicts no trade at all — yet such trade happens in real life. Ricardo filled this gap.
concepts.analogy: A fast cook and a fast typist living together: the cook cooks, the typist types, and both finish earlier.
concepts.work: Sourcing decisions often begin with a simple absolute-cost comparison — which country makes this component cheapest? A CA preparing a make-or-import analysis starts here before adding duties, freight and currency.

concepts.title: Comparative advantage — David Ricardo (and Haberler)
body: Ricardo showed that what matters is relative (comparative) cost, not absolute cost. Even if one country is more efficient in every good, both countries gain when each specialises in the good where its advantage is greatest (or its disadvantage is smallest) and imports the other.

Test: compare opportunity costs. The country whose opportunity cost of a good is lower has the comparative advantage in it. Terms of trade must lie between the two countries' home cost ratios for both to gain.

Ricardo built the theory on the labour theory of value (labour as the only factor). Gottfried Haberler later restated it with opportunity cost — the value of the alternative given up — so the theory no longer depends on labour alone.

Comparative advantage makes trade a positive-sum game: total output and living standards rise in both countries. It also applies to services such as software or financial products. A developing country without absolute advantage in anything will still have a comparative advantage in something.
concepts.analogy: A senior partner who types faster than her assistant still lets the assistant type — her time is worth more spent on client advice. Her comparative advantage is advice; his is typing.
concepts.work: The same logic guides outsourcing and shared-service decisions in firms: keep in-house what you are relatively best at, buy the rest. CAs use opportunity-cost reasoning in every make-or-buy and capacity-allocation decision.

concepts.title: Heckscher-Ohlin (factor endowment / modern) theory
body: Swedish economists Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin explained why comparative costs differ: countries are endowed with different amounts of factors (labour, capital, land).

A country exports goods whose production uses its relatively abundant factor intensively and imports goods that use its relatively scarce factor intensively. Capital-rich countries export capital-intensive goods; labour-rich countries export labour-intensive goods.
Factor-price equalisation theorem: free trade tends to equalise factor prices — wages and returns on capital move closer across trading countries.

Compared with Ricardo: the modern theory is a two-factor (extendable) model based on money costs; it explains the cause of comparative advantage (factor endowments and factor prices); it treats international trade as a special case of inter-regional trade; and it is positive (explains the basis of trade) while the classical theory is normative (shows the gains). It cannot explain intra-industry trade — countries exporting and importing similar goods.
concepts.analogy: A farm with lots of land grows wheat; a crowded city with many hands stitches shirts. Each sells what its surroundings make cheap.
concepts.work: Investors and policy makers use factor-endowment reasoning to judge which Indian sectors (labour-intensive textiles, leather, assembly) can compete globally — useful when a CA evaluates a client's export project.

concepts.title: New trade theory — scale, variety and network effects
body: New trade theory (NTT) emerged in the late 1970s and 1980s. Paul Krugman (Nobel Prize 2008) noticed that most world trade takes place between countries with similar capital-labour ratios — rich countries trading cars with each other — which Heckscher-Ohlin cannot explain.

NTT adds imperfect competition and increasing returns. Economies of scale: a firm selling to home and foreign markets produces more, so its cost per unit falls. Network effects: a product becomes more valuable as more people use it (the "bandwagon effect") — messaging apps and computer operating systems.

Trade still remains positive-sum; NTT adds extra gains from bigger markets, more competition, more product variety and cheaper, better intermediate and capital inputs. It explains intra-industry trade (a country exporting household refrigerators while importing industrial coolers) and the large trade between developed and big developing economies (such as BRICS) in similar products.

NTT also points out that markets dominated by a few large firms with scale economies can lead to results that are not the best possible for society (sub-optimal), unlike the classical picture of a perfectly efficient world economy.
concepts.analogy: One messaging app wins because everyone is on it — the more users, the more useful, the cheaper per user. Size itself becomes an advantage.
concepts.work: Valuation and equity research on platform and manufacturing companies leans heavily on scale economies and network effects — the same forces NTT uses to explain trade patterns.

(b) Find the opportunity cost of each good in each country and state which good each should export. (c) Within what range must the terms of trade (cloth per unit of wheat) lie? illustrations.title: Opportunity cost from production possibilities (Haberler)
illustrations.q: Using all its resources, Country X can make either 100 phones or 400 kg of coffee; Country Y can make either 60 phones or 120 kg of coffee (constant costs). Which country has the comparative advantage in phones and which in coffee?

solution.text: Phones: Y gives up only 2 kg of coffee per phone against 4 kg in X, so Y has the comparative advantage in phones. Coffee: X gives up only 0.25 phone per kg against 0.5 in Y, so X has the comparative advantage in coffee.
X can make more of both goods (absolute advantage in both), yet Y still has a comparative advantage. Haberler's opportunity-cost version needs no labour theory of value — any mix of factors works.

illustrations.title: Factor endowments decide exports (Heckscher-Ohlin)
illustrations.q: Kestria has 800 units of capital and 200 units of labour. Lumina has 300 units of capital and 600 units of labour. Machine tools are capital-intensive and readymade garments are labour-intensive. Using the Heckscher-Ohlin theory, predict the pattern of trade and the effect on factor prices.

solution.text: A country exports the good that uses its abundant (and therefore cheap) factor intensively and imports the good that uses its scarce factor intensively.

Factor-price equalisation: as Lumina exports more garments, demand for its labour rises and wages go up; in Kestria the return to capital rises. Free trade pushes wages and returns to capital in the two countries towards each other.

checks.label: Kestria: capital per worker
Lumina: capital per worker

jobs.title: Make in India or import? An opportunity-cost view
jobs.role: CA in industry (plant controller of an electronics assembler)
jobs.situation: Your plant can make either control boards or wiring harnesses on the same line. Management wants to make both because "we are better than the overseas supplier at both".
steps: Measure line-hours per unit for each product and compare with landed import prices.
Work out the opportunity cost: how many harnesses are given up for each board made.
Allocate scarce line-hours to the product with the larger relative advantage; import the other if the landed price is below your opportunity cost.
Present the profit difference to management with a sensitivity for duty and exchange rate.
jobs.takeaway: Being better at everything does not mean you should make everything — scarce capacity should go where the relative advantage is largest.
jobs.think: Line-hours: board 2, harness 1. A harness can be imported for a price equal to the contribution from 0.4 board. Should you import harnesses?
jobs.answer: Making one harness costs 1 line-hour = 0.5 board forgone. Buying it costs only 0.4 board, which is less than the 0.5 board given up, so importing harnesses and using the line for boards is better.

jobs.title: Reading a sector's export potential
jobs.role: Research analyst at a broking firm
jobs.situation: You are asked whether an Indian footwear company can keep growing exports to Europe.
steps: Check factor intensity: footwear is labour-intensive — India's abundant factor (Heckscher-Ohlin).
Check scale: large plants lower unit cost (new trade theory).
Check the case against trade: dependence on one market, sudden standards or tariff changes.
Conclude with risks and a view on margins.
jobs.takeaway: Trade theories give a quick, structured first view of whether a sector's export story is sustainable.

mcqs.q: Which feature is NOT a difference between internal trade and international trade?
options: Use of a single common currency and uniform laws in both
Factors of production are less mobile across borders
mcqs.explain: International trade involves several currencies, different legal systems and less mobility of labour and capital across borders. A single common currency with uniform laws describes internal trade, so it is not a difference — it is the exception. 'Factors are less mobile across borders' is tempting to reject, but it is a real distinguishing feature. In practice: an Indian exporter must handle foreign-exchange conversion, FEMA rules and foreign contract law, which a domestic seller never faces.
mcqs.topic: International trade, its gains and the case against it

mcqs.q: Mercantilists believed a nation becomes wealthy and powerful by:
options: Maximising exports and minimising imports to accumulate precious metals
Free trade with no state control
mcqs.explain: Mercantilists (16th–18th century Europe) believed national wealth and power came from piling up gold and silver, so they pushed for maximum exports, minimum imports and a permanent trade surplus, backed by high tariffs. 'Specialising according to comparative cost' is the trap — that is Ricardo's later free-trade idea. In practice: modern calls to treat any trade deficit as a national loss echo mercantilist thinking that economists caution against.
mcqs.topic: Mercantilism — trade as a way to pile up gold

mcqs.q: Under mercantilism, trade was viewed as:
mcqs.explain: Mercantilists saw world wealth as fixed, so one nation's gain from trade had to be another's loss — a zero-sum game. 'A positive-sum game' is the trap: that is the classical view from comparative advantage, where both partners can gain. In practice: trade negotiators who argue that every bilateral surplus is a 'win' and every deficit a 'loss' are using a zero-sum mindset that modern economics rejects.
mcqs.topic: Mercantilism — trade as a way to pile up gold

mcqs.q: The theory of absolute advantage was given by:
mcqs.explain: Adam Smith, in The Wealth of Nations (1776), argued that countries gain by specialising in goods they produce at an absolutely lower cost and trading for the rest. David Ricardo is the trap — he developed comparative advantage, which builds on and improves Smith's idea. In practice: India's large export of IT services, where it is highly efficient, is often explained using Smith-style specialisation in a simplified way.

mcqs.q: According to the absolute advantage theory, if one country is more efficient in both goods:
options: The efficient country imports both goods
mcqs.explain: Smith's theory needs each country to be absolutely better at one good. If one country is more efficient in both, the theory predicts no trade. 'Both countries will still trade' is the tempting answer — that is true, but it comes from Ricardo's comparative advantage, which removed this limitation. In practice: rich countries still import from less efficient poorer countries, showing that comparative, not absolute, advantage drives real trade.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT an assumption of Adam Smith's absolute advantage theory?
options: Costs are measured by labour required
mcqs.explain: Smith assumed labour moves freely within a country but cannot move between countries; trade in goods substitutes for that immobility. The other assumptions — two countries and two goods, no transport costs, and costs measured in labour — are genuine. 'No transport costs' is a tempting pick because it sounds unrealistic, but it is assumed. In practice: visa restrictions limit labour movement, which is why Indian talent is often exported indirectly through IT services.

mcqs.q: Comparative advantage means a country can produce a good:
options: At a lower opportunity cost than another country
With fewer labour hours than every other country
mcqs.explain: Comparative advantage means a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost — giving up less of other goods — than its trading partner. 'With fewer labour hours than every other country' is the trap: that is absolute advantage. A country can have comparative advantage even if it is less efficient in everything. In practice: India exports textiles and gems partly because their opportunity cost here is lower, not because India is best at everything.

mcqs.q: Ricardo explained comparative advantage on the basis of:
mcqs.explain: Ricardo built comparative cost theory on the labour theory of value — the cost of a good is measured by the labour needed to produce it. 'Opportunity cost' is the trap: Gottfried Haberler later restated the theory in opportunity-cost terms, freeing it from dependence on labour alone. In practice: introductory trade analysis still often starts with labour-hour tables like Ricardo's before moving to more realistic models.

mcqs.q: Who restated the comparative cost theory in terms of opportunity cost?
mcqs.explain: Gottfried Haberler restated comparative cost theory using opportunity cost, so it no longer depended on labour being the only factor of production. Eli Heckscher is the trap — he co-founded the factor-endowment theory with Ohlin. Adam Smith gave absolute advantage. In practice: opportunity-cost reasoning is what business consultants and economists use today when advising which products a firm or country should focus on.

mcqs.q: According to the theory of comparative advantage, trade is:
options: A positive-sum game — the net gain to the participants is positive
Beneficial only to the more efficient country
Beneficial only when transport cost is zero
mcqs.explain: Under comparative advantage, each country specialises in what it produces at lower opportunity cost, world output rises, and both can consume more — a positive-sum game. 'A zero-sum game' is the trap: that was the mercantilist view. Gains do not require zero transport costs, only that costs are low enough. In practice: trade agreements, such as India's with the UAE, are justified by these mutual gains.

mcqs.q: Labour hours per unit — A: cloth 30, grain 60; B: cloth 60, grain 30. Which country should produce grain?
mcqs.explain: Grain needs 60 hours in A but only 30 in B, so B has the absolute advantage in grain — and also the comparative advantage, since grain costs B 0.5 cloth against 2 cloth in A. A makes cloth with 30 hours against B's 60. 'Country A' is the trap — A is better at cloth, not grain. In practice: this simple labour-hour comparison mirrors how analysts compare unit production costs across countries.

mcqs.q: Labour hours per unit — India: tables 4, mats 2; Bangladesh: tables 10, mats 1. Which statement is correct?
options: All three of the others are true
Bangladesh has a comparative advantage in mats
India has a comparative advantage in tables
Bangladesh has an absolute advantage in mats
mcqs.explain: Opportunity cost of a table: India 4 ÷ 2 = 2 mats; Bangladesh 10 ÷ 1 = 10 mats, so India has the comparative advantage in tables and Bangladesh in mats. Bangladesh needs 1 hour per mat against India's 2, so it also has the absolute advantage in mats. All three statements hold; picking just one is the trap. In practice: trade economists compute such ratios using real cost data.

mcqs.q: Labour hours per unit — X: wheat 10, rice 20; Y: wheat 20, rice 10. They specialise and trade 1 wheat for 1 rice. How many labour hours does X gain per unit of rice imported?
mcqs.explain: X specialises in wheat (10 hours) and trades 1 wheat for 1 rice. Producing that rice at home would take 20 hours, so X saves 20 − 10 = 10 labour hours per unit of rice imported. The tempting 20 hours forgets that X spent 10 hours making the wheat it exported; 30 adds the two. In practice: firms make the same make-or-buy comparison when deciding whether to outsource a component.

mcqs.q: Country P needs 3 hours for wheat and 6 for cloth; Q needs 9 hours for wheat and 12 for cloth. The opportunity cost of 1 unit of wheat in Q (in cloth) is:
mcqs.explain: In Q, 1 wheat takes 9 hours and 1 cloth 12 hours, so producing 1 wheat means giving up 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 cloth. The tempting 0.5 is P's opportunity cost (3 ÷ 6); 1.33 (12 ÷ 9) and 2 (6 ÷ 3) are the costs of cloth in wheat. In practice: getting the ratio the right way up — cost of the good in terms of the other good — is the most common exam slip.

mcqs.q: With the data of the previous question, mutually beneficial terms of trade (cloth per wheat) must lie between:
mcqs.explain: Trade benefits both only if the terms of trade lie between the two domestic opportunity costs: P's 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 and Q's 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 cloth per wheat. P gains by getting more than 0.5 cloth, and Q gains by paying less than 0.75. 'Between 0.5 and 2' is the trap, mixing ratios measured in different units. In practice: trade negotiators bargain over where within such a range the actual price settles.

mcqs.q: With all its resources Country X can make 100 phones or 400 kg coffee; Y can make 60 phones or 120 kg coffee. The opportunity cost of one phone in Y is:
mcqs.explain: Y can make 60 phones or 120 kg coffee, so one phone costs 120 ÷ 60 = 2 kg coffee. The tempting 4 kg is X's opportunity cost (400 ÷ 100). 0.5 and 0.25 phone are coffee costs in phone terms. Since Y gives up less coffee per phone, Y has the comparative advantage in phones. In practice: production-possibility data like this help economists identify which sectors a country should export.

mcqs.q: The Heckscher-Ohlin theory says comparative advantage arises from differences in:
mcqs.explain: The Heckscher-Ohlin (factor-endowment or modern) theory says comparative advantage arises from differences in countries' endowments of factors such as labour, capital and land. 'Labour productivity alone' is the trap — that is the Ricardian explanation. Economies of scale belong to new trade theory. In practice: India's labour abundance helps explain its exports of labour-intensive goods such as garments and leather products.

mcqs.q: A labour-abundant country will, according to Heckscher-Ohlin, export:
mcqs.explain: Under Heckscher-Ohlin, a country exports goods that use its relatively abundant, and therefore cheap, factor intensively. A labour-abundant country exports labour-intensive goods. 'Capital-intensive goods' is the trap — those would be exported by a capital-rich country. In practice: Bangladesh and Vietnam, with abundant labour, have become major garment exporters, consistent with this theory.

mcqs.q: The factor-price equalisation theorem states that free trade:
options: Tends to equalise wages and returns on capital across trading countries
Equalises the prices of all goods within a country
Makes labour fully mobile between countries
Raises wages only in the capital-rich country
mcqs.explain: The factor-price equalisation theorem says free trade raises demand for each country's abundant factor and lowers demand for its scarce factor, so wages and returns to capital tend to converge across trading countries. 'Makes labour fully mobile between countries' is the trap — trade in goods substitutes for factor movement. In practice: wage pressure in rich-country manufacturing from low-cost imports is often explained with this theorem.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE of the modern (Heckscher-Ohlin) theory compared with the classical comparative cost theory?
options: It explains the cause of comparative cost differences
It is based on the labour theory of value
It treats international trade as entirely different from domestic trade
mcqs.explain: The modern Heckscher-Ohlin theory explains why comparative costs differ — because of differences in factor endowments. The classical theory only assumed cost differences. The other options — labour theory of value, treating trade as entirely different from domestic trade, and a one-factor model — describe the classical theory, which is the trap. In practice: economists use factor-endowment analysis to predict export patterns of developing countries.

mcqs.q: The classical comparative cost theory is best described as:
options: Normative — it demonstrates the gains from trade
Positive — it explains the basis of trade
mcqs.explain: The classical comparative cost theory is normative: it demonstrates the gains from trade and argues that free trade is beneficial. The modern Heckscher-Ohlin theory is positive, explaining the basis of trade. 'Positive — explains the basis of trade' is the trap, swapping the two. It is also a one-factor model based on labour costs, not money costs. In practice: free-trade advocacy relies on the classical theory's demonstration of gains.

mcqs.q: Paul Krugman noticed that most world trade takes place between countries that:
mcqs.explain: Paul Krugman observed that most world trade happens between countries with similar capital–labour ratios — for example, rich countries trading cars with each other. 'Very different factor endowments' is the trap: that is what Heckscher-Ohlin would predict, and the mismatch with reality led to new trade theory. In practice: India's growing two-way trade in auto components with Europe and Japan fits this pattern.
mcqs.topic: New trade theory — scale, variety and network effects

mcqs.q: A country exports household refrigerators and imports industrial coolers. This is:
options: Inter-industry trade explained by factor endowments
mcqs.explain: Exporting household refrigerators while importing industrial coolers is two-way trade in similar products within one industry — intra-industry trade, explained by product variety and economies of scale. 'Inter-industry trade explained by factor endowments' is the trap — that involves exchanging different kinds of goods, like garments for machinery. In practice: India both exports and imports cars and pharmaceuticals, a common feature of intra-industry trade.
mcqs.topic: New trade theory — scale, variety and network effects

mcqs.q: The value of a messaging app to each user rises as more people use it. New trade theory calls this:
mcqs.explain: When each user's value rises as more people use a product, it is a network effect (also called a bandwagon effect). 'A diseconomy of scale' is the trap — that is rising average cost as a firm grows, the opposite of increasing benefits. In practice: UPI and messaging apps such as WhatsApp became dominant in India because each new user made the network more valuable for everyone else.
mcqs.topic: New trade theory — scale, variety and network effects

mcqs.q: Which pair of ideas is central to new trade theory?
options: Economies of scale and network effects
Labour theory of value and absolute cost
mcqs.explain: New trade theory emphasises economies of scale (increasing returns) and network effects, along with imperfect competition, to explain trade between similar countries and first-mover advantages. 'Factor endowment and factor-price equalisation' is the trap — those are Heckscher-Ohlin ideas. Precious metals and surpluses belong to mercantilism. In practice: India's Production Linked Incentive schemes aim to help firms reach global scale in electronics and solar manufacturing.
mcqs.topic: New trade theory — scale, variety and network effects

mcqs.q: Paul Krugman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in:
mcqs.explain: Paul Krugman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2008 for his analysis of trade patterns and the location of economic activity (economic geography). 1998 is the trap — that year's prize went to Amartya Sen for welfare economics. In practice: Krugman's work on scale and clustering helps explain why industries concentrate in hubs such as Bengaluru for IT or Tiruppur for knitwear.
mcqs.topic: New trade theory — scale, variety and network effects

mcqs.q: Which is an argument AGAINST unrestricted trade?
options: Business cycles and crises spread quickly between countries
It earns foreign exchange for imports
mcqs.explain: Unrestricted trade links economies so closely that business cycles and financial crises spread quickly from one country to another — an argument against it. Weakening domestic monopolies, more variety for consumers and foreign-exchange earnings are traps: they are benefits of trade. In practice: the 2008 global financial crisis hit Indian exports and capital flows within months, showing how integration transmits shocks.
mcqs.topic: International trade, its gains and the case against it

mcqs.q: Country P: wheat 3 hours, cloth 6 hours; Q: wheat 9 hours, cloth 12 hours. At 1 wheat = 0.6 cloth, how many hours does Q save on each unit of wheat it imports?
mcqs.explain: Q imports wheat at 1 wheat = 0.6 cloth. The cloth Q gives up costs 0.6 × 12 = 7.2 hours, while producing wheat at home would take 9 hours, so Q saves 9 − 7.2 = 1.8 hours per unit. The tempting 1 hour is P's saving on each unit of cloth it imports. In practice: such calculations show how gains from trade are shared depending on the agreed exchange rate.

viva.q: State the theory of comparative advantage.
viva.model: David Ricardo said that a country should specialise in and export the good in which it has a comparative advantage, that is a lower opportunity cost or a smaller relative disadvantage, and import the other good. Even if one country has an absolute advantage in both goods, both countries still gain from trade.

viva.q: What did Adam Smith say about the basis of international trade?
viva.model: Adam Smith said trade is based on absolute advantage. A country should specialise in the good it can produce with less labour than the other country and exchange it for the good the other country makes more cheaply, so both gain. If one country is not better at any good, his theory predicts no trade.

viva.q: Explain the Heckscher-Ohlin theory of trade.
viva.model: The Heckscher-Ohlin theory, also called the factor endowment theory, says comparative advantage comes from differences in factor endowments. A country exports goods that use its relatively abundant factor intensively and imports goods that use its scarce factor intensively. So a capital-rich country exports capital-intensive goods and a labour-rich country exports labour-intensive goods, and trade tends to equalise factor prices.

viva.q: What was the mercantilist view of international trade?
viva.model: Mercantilists, who dominated Europe from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century, believed national wealth meant holding gold and silver. So a country should maximise exports and minimise imports, using high tariffs and state control, to keep a trade surplus. They saw trade as a zero-sum game.

viva.q: How does the new trade theory explain trade between similar countries?
viva.model: New trade theory, linked with Paul Krugman, says much trade is between countries with similar factor endowments. It is driven by economies of scale, where cost per unit falls as a firm sells in more markets, and by network effects, where a product becomes more valuable as more people use it. This explains intra-industry trade in similar products.

cases.title: Sundar and Vellora negotiate a trade deal
cases.case: Two countries are planning a bilateral deal. In Sundar a worker-day produces 4 tonnes of steel or 8 lots of garments. In Vellora a worker-day produces 3 tonnes of steel or 12 lots of garments. Sundar has relatively more capital per worker; Vellora has relatively more labour. A minister in Sundar argues that "we should only export and never import, so that our reserves keep rising".

mcqs.q: What is the opportunity cost of one tonne of steel in Vellora (in lots of garments)?
mcqs.explain: In Vellora, one worker-day produces 3 tonnes of steel or 12 lots of garments, so one tonne of steel costs 12 ÷ 3 = 4 lots of garments. The tempting 2 is Sundar's opportunity cost (8 ÷ 4); 0.25 is the cost of a garment lot in tonnes of steel in Vellora. In practice: trade negotiators begin with such opportunity costs to decide which sectors each country should concentrate on.

mcqs.q: Which pattern of specialisation benefits both countries?
options: Sundar exports steel; Vellora exports garments
Sundar exports garments; Vellora exports steel
No trade — Sundar is better at steel only
mcqs.explain: Steel costs 2 lots of garments in Sundar but 4 in Vellora, so Sundar has the comparative advantage in steel. A garment lot costs 0.25 tonne of steel in Vellora and 0.5 tonne in Sundar, so Vellora has it in garments. 'No trade — Sundar is better at steel only' is the trap, applying absolute advantage. In practice: such specialisation is the economic basis of bilateral trade deals.

mcqs.q: The factor data (Sundar capital-rich, Vellora labour-rich) supports this pattern under which theory?
mcqs.explain: Capital-rich Sundar exports capital-intensive steel, and labour-rich Vellora exports labour-intensive garments — exactly the Heckscher-Ohlin prediction that countries export goods using their abundant factor intensively. 'Absolute advantage only' is the trap, since the question links trade to factor endowments, not just efficiency. In practice: India's exports of labour-intensive garments and imports of capital goods fit this pattern.

mcqs.q: The minister's view reflects which school of thought?
mcqs.explain: The minister wants to export only and never import so that reserves keep rising — the mercantilist goal of accumulating precious metals or reserves through a permanent surplus. 'Comparative advantage' is the trap: that theory says imports are as beneficial as exports. In practice: excessive reserve hoarding has an opportunity cost, since those resources could have bought imports that raise living standards or investment.
mcqs.topic: Mercantilism — trade as a way to pile up gold

mcqs.q: Which terms of trade (lots of garments per tonne of steel) would benefit both countries?
mcqs.explain: Both countries gain only if the terms of trade lie strictly between their opportunity costs of steel: Sundar's 2 and Vellora's 4 lots of garments per tonne. Only 3 lies inside that range. At exactly 2 Sundar gains nothing; 1.5 hurts Sundar; 5 hurts Vellora. In practice: in real negotiations, the final terms within this range depend on bargaining power and demand in each country.
